sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
July 2026 delivered a tale of two tapes across global equity markets. US equities experienced significant intramonth turbulence driven by a sharp correction in technology and semiconductor names, while European and select APAC bourses posted solid gains as investor rotation sought value, cyclicals, and geographies less exposed to AI capex concerns.

Beneath the surface of broadly mixed headline returns, the month was defined by a seismic shift in market leadership. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) recorded its worst monthly performance since 2008, declining **-20.6%**, while the Nasdaq 100 fell **-6.6%**. In contrast, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose **+0.6%** — its fourth consecutive winning month — and the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index gained **+1.0%**, highlighting a broadening of market participation away from mega-cap technology.

Cross-regional performance was similarly divergent: Germany's DAX surged **+4.8%** to close at **25,629.24**, and the FTSE 100 advanced **+4.5%** to end at **8,509.64**, while US large-cap benchmarks struggled to hold ground amid the tech unwind. Gold reached a monthly close of **$4,046.84/oz** — its best month since February — as geopolitical tensions and policy uncertainty drove safe-haven demand.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
AI Mega-Cap Correction and Late-Month Reversal -- The singular drama of July was the violent unwinding of the AI-driven semiconductor trade. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) collapsed **-20.6%** — its steepest monthly decline since 2008 — as investors grappled with concerns over AI capex monetisation, expanding competitive dynamics, and the sustainability of hyperscaler valuations after a record Q2. The Nasdaq 100 fell **-6.6%** over the month as multiple compression ran well ahead of any fundamental deterioration in underlying businesses.

The narrative shifted decisively in the final week, however, as Microsoft, Amazon, and other hyperscalers reported Q2 results that reaffirmed accelerating cloud and AI revenues: Micron Technology surged **+18%** and Advanced Micro Devices gained **+13%** in the closing sessions, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF recovered **+8%** off its intramonth lows. Despite the drawdown, the SOX remained up **+59.7%** year-to-date through July — underscoring the extent to which valuations had stretched ahead of the reset, and signalling that the AI structural story remained intact even as near-term positioning required a reset.

Middle East Escalation and Oil Shock -- Geopolitical risk re-entered the market calculus sharply in July as President Trump declared an end to the fragile ceasefire in the Strait of Hormuz, triggering a **+7%** single-session spike in crude oil benchmarks. Brent crude advanced from approximately **$76.80/bbl** in early July to approximately **$90–92/bbl** by month-end (approx., verify before merging) — a rise of roughly **+12%** that marked crude's strongest monthly performance in over a year. The market dislocation on the day of the announcement sent the Dow Jones Industrial Average tumbling more than **800 points**, or approximately **-1.5%**, despite the index having set a record high just two sessions earlier.

The conflict introduced fresh uncertainty into an already complex macro backdrop. The International Monetary Fund downgraded its 2026 global growth forecast to **3.0%**, warning that renewed conflict in the Middle East threatens supply chains, sustains commodity price volatility, and risks re-igniting inflationary pressures that had only partially abated. Energy sector equities outperformed amid the crude rally, providing a partial offset to the technology-led drawdown in US indices and contributing to the relative outperformance of value-tilted benchmarks for the month.

Growth-to-Value Rotation and Broadening Market Participation -- July's equity dynamics underscored a structural shift in investor preference from AI-adjacent growth to value, cyclicals, and international equities. While the Nasdaq 100 declined **-6.6%** and the S&P 500 posted approximately flat performance (approx., verify before merging), the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index gained **+1.0%**, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose **+0.6%**, and European markets outperformed materially. Sector leadership rotated toward industrials, autos, real estate, and basic resources, with Autos & Parts gaining approximately **+4.6%** and Retail and Real Estate each advancing approximately **+3.2%**.

A Bank of America fund manager survey highlighted that European equity positioning improved markedly in July — net overweight allocations recovering sharply from the prior month's underweight — validating the cross-regional rotation. Consumer spending proved resilient across developed markets, PMI readings improved, and productivity growth remained strong, providing a fundamental backdrop for the cyclical re-rating. This rotation dynamic is likely to persist into H2 2026 if AI earnings results continue to validate, reducing the binary thematic risk that had dominated the first half.

Federal Reserve's Hawkish Hold and Yield Surge -- The Federal Open Market Committee voted **9-3** on July 29 to maintain the federal funds rate in the **3.50%–3.75%** target range, with three regional presidents — Cleveland, Minneapolis, and Dallas — dissenting in favour of an immediate hike, citing inflation that has remained above the **2%** target for more than five consecutive years. The divided vote and accompanying statement underscored the Fed's discomfort with the current equilibrium: resilient activity and strong productivity growth on one side, stubborn inflation amplified by Middle East-driven energy costs on the other.

US Treasury yields rose sharply in response: the 10-year yield eclipsed **4.60%** on July 21 and closed the month at **4.75%**, while the 2-year yield settled at **4.28%**, reflecting a meaningful re-pricing of the rate path. Markets moved to price in two additional **25 basis-point** hikes for 2026, with no easing envisaged through 2027. The steepening yield environment amplified the de-rating of long-duration growth assets, compounding the semiconductor correction and reinforcing the rotation into financials and shorter-duration value equities.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equity markets delivered a sharply bifurcated performance in July. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained **+0.6%** to close at **52,485.03** — its fourth consecutive monthly advance — while the S&P 500 finished approximately flat (approx., verify before merging) at **7,489.72**. The Nasdaq Composite fell to **25,373.85**, with the Nasdaq 100 posting a **-6.6%** monthly loss as the AI-semiconductor complex bore the brunt of a positioning unwind that drove the SOX to its worst month since 2008 at **-20.6%**.

The underlying sector dynamics were more constructive than headline indices suggest. Value and cyclical sectors — autos, retail, real estate, and basic resources — all advanced meaningfully as investors rotated into cheaper, income-generating equities with less AI valuation exposure. The Federal Reserve's July 29 hold at **3.50%–3.75%** on a **9-3** vote weighed initially on sentiment given the hawkish dissent, but late-month hyperscaler earnings from Microsoft and Amazon restored confidence in the AI capex thesis, triggering a sharp recovery in semiconductor names.

Q2 earnings season broadly supported the fundamental case for continued expansion: consumer spending remained resilient, labour markets held firm, and productivity growth stayed strong. The Nasdaq Composite's **+1%** advance on the final trading day of the month and the iShares Semiconductor ETF's **+8%** bounce off its lows provided a constructive handoff into August, with sentiment positioned to recover as earnings validation accumulated.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities significantly outperformed their US counterparts in July, with Germany's DAX and the UK's FTSE 100 leading a broadly positive tape. The DAX surged **+4.8%** to close at **25,629.24**, reaching fresh record territory driven by resilient corporate earnings, a moderation in rate concerns, and improving fund-flow dynamics from global investors rotating away from US mega-cap technology. The FTSE 100 advanced **+4.5%** to **8,509.64**, buoyed by energy sector gains from the crude price rally and the UK's structurally lower exposure to AI valuation risk. France's CAC 40 gained approximately **+0.9%** (approx., verify before merging) as chemical, retail, and industrial sectors outperformed.

The outperformance reflected a convergence of structural and cyclical tailwinds. A Bank of America fund manager survey showed a notable improvement in European equity positioning in July, with net overweight allocations recovering from deep underweight levels the prior month — signalling the early stages of a structural rotation that European strategists had long anticipated. PMI readings across Germany, France, and the UK improved, and corporate earnings in the industrial, auto, and chemicals sectors broadly beat expectations.

The European Central Bank's September meeting loomed as the next key catalyst. While Middle East-driven energy cost pressures complicated the easing path, stronger-than-expected GDP data gave policymakers some flexibility. The Stoxx 600's year-to-date advance to approximately **+11%** — achieved without the concentrated AI single-stock risk that characterised US indices — underscores the durability of Europe's recovery and its relative attractiveness as portfolio rotation accelerates.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets presented a mixed picture in July, with Japan's Nikkei 225 delivering the most dramatic intramonth narrative. A magnitude **7.5** earthquake north of Tokyo on July 28–29 triggered a sharp **-1.34%** single-session decline, but the index recovered forcefully on July 31 — advancing **+4.03%** to close at **64,362.02** — as the Bank of Japan held its policy rate at **1.0%** and the yen strengthened following suspected Ministry of Finance intervention. For the calendar month overall, the Nikkei's performance was roughly flat to modestly negative (approx., verify before merging), reflecting the intramonth earthquake shock offset by the strong final-session surge; the index remained up approximately **+33.6%** year-to-date through mid-July.

The Bank of Japan's July 31 policy meeting was the region's most closely watched macro event: the BoJ held rates at **1.0%** — the highest since September 1995 — following a **+25 basis point** hike in June, signalling continued gradualism in normalisation. USD/JPY oscillated in the **157–160** range during the session, with the yen strengthening from **159.53** to approximately **157.39** in what multiple sources attributed to suspected Ministry of Finance FX intervention ahead of the announcement.

Chinese equities underperformed, with the Hang Seng posting a modest approximately **+0.2%** gain for the month (approx., verify before merging) while the Shanghai Composite edged lower, closing near **3,804** on July 30. Chip-related stocks weighed on mainland indices ahead of the Politburo meeting, and the divergence between offshore Hong Kong equities and onshore Shanghai names persisted, with the SSE Composite carrying year-to-date losses of approximately **-1.4%** as investors remained cautious on the domestic growth trajectory.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar strengthened broadly in July, with the DXY Dollar Index trading in a wide **98.84–102.68** intramonth range as Middle East risk premia, hawkish Fed signals, and episodic risk-off dynamics drove demand for dollar assets. The index ended the month near the upper portion of its range at approximately **101** (approx., verify before merging), representing an advance of roughly **+2.6%** over the 30-day window — consistent with the dollar's historical pattern of benefiting from geopolitical uncertainty and yield differentials.

EUR/USD drifted lower over the month, settling near approximately **1.1438** — a decline of roughly **-1.0%** — as investors weighed the ECB's complicated disinflation path against higher European energy costs from the crude rally. GBP/USD held relatively firm at approximately **1.33** at month-end, supported by resilient UK economic data and the FTSE 100's strong performance attracting foreign inflows. The most volatile pair was USD/JPY, which surged to the **160** handle before a sharp reversal on July 31 attributed to suspected Bank of Japan intervention, ultimately settling near **157.39** as the BoJ held rates at **1.0%**.

The yen's late-July intervention episode underscored persistent structural tensions in G10 FX: the BoJ's reluctance to accelerate the rate-hike cycle despite yen weakness creates a recurring vulnerability that markets will continue to test through year-end. The broader dollar rally during July reflected a re-pricing of Fed rate-cut expectations, with markets now pricing two additional **25 basis-point** hikes and no easing through 2027.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Commodities delivered exceptional performance in July, with crude oil and copper leading the gains. Brent crude advanced from approximately **$76.80/bbl** in early July to approximately **$90–92/bbl** by month-end (approx., verify before merging) — a rise of roughly **+12%** that represented the benchmark's strongest monthly advance in over a year. The move was catalysed by the collapse of the Strait of Hormuz ceasefire, which triggered a single-session **+7%** spike and forced a broad re-pricing of geopolitical risk premium across energy markets. WTI crude tracked Brent's trajectory closely throughout the month.

Gold delivered its best month since February, closing July 31 at **$4,046.84/oz** after trading in a wide intraday range of **$4,028.59–$4,078.92**. The metal was supported by the convergence of geopolitical uncertainty, the inflation-hedge demand reignited by the crude spike, and a flight-to-safety bid at the peak of the Middle East escalation. Gold's continued ascent — reaching approximately **$4,400/oz** by mid-August — confirmed the metal's structural uptrend remained firmly intact.

Copper was a standout performer, with COMEX contracts settling at **$6.376/lb** on July 29, up **+3.3%** for the month. US import data showed more than **200,000 tonnes** of refined copper arriving at US ports in July — the largest monthly inflow since records began in 2014 — as traders continued frontloading shipments ahead of anticipated US tariffs. The COMEX-LME premium held at approximately **19 cents/lb**, or roughly **8.4 times** its long-run historical average, reflecting sustained tariff-arbitrage positioning.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
US Treasury markets experienced meaningful yield pressure in July, with the 10-year benchmark breaching **4.60%** on July 21 and closing the month at **4.75%** — one of the highest readings of the current rate cycle. The 2-year yield settled at **4.28%** by July 31, reflecting re-pricing of the Fed's near-term policy trajectory. Starting the month at approximately **4.50%** (approx., verify before merging), the 10-year yield's approximately **+25 basis point** advance over July reflected a combination of oil-driven inflation concerns, elevated geopolitical risk premium, and the Fed's unmistakably hawkish policy stance.

The Federal Open Market Committee voted **9-3** on July 29 to hold the federal funds rate in the **3.50%–3.75%** range, with three regional Fed presidents dissenting in favour of an immediate hike — citing inflation above the **2%** target for more than five years. The divided vote and the Committee's statement, which noted that geopolitical risks and energy price pressures remained unresolved, reinforced market pricing of two additional **25 basis-point** hikes in 2026 with no easing through 2027.

The rising yield environment created compound headwinds for risk assets: higher discount rates amplified the de-rating of long-duration growth equities (deepening the tech selloff), while simultaneously supporting financial sector stocks and providing income-oriented investors with more attractive entry points across the Treasury curve. Credit spreads remained relatively contained despite the rate volatility, suggesting that fundamental credit quality held firm even as the rate path turned more hawkish than markets had anticipated entering the month.
